prompt: Order these mapping innovations from earliest to most recent.

options.text: Mercator publishes cylindrical sea chart
GPS satellites broadcast location signals
Ptolemy compiles Geographia world atlas
Airplanes capture stereo aerial photos

explanation: Ptolemy wrote Geographia around 150 CE, Mercator mapped in 1569, aerial photos grew in the 1910s, and GPS began in 1978.

trap_notes.default: Anchor ancient atlases before Renaissance sea charts, then 20th-century aviation before space-age satellites.

prompt: Order the four classic stages of the Demographic Transition Model.

options.text: Death rates drop while birth rates stay high
Both birth and death rates stabilize low
Both birth and death rates remain high
Birth rates fall toward low death rates

explanation: In the Demographic Transition Model, death rates fall in Stage 2 before birth rates decline in Stage 3 and stabilize in Stage 4.

trap_notes.default: Remember that improved sanitation lowers death rates first; families reduce birth rates later.

prompt: Order these major human migration waves from earliest to latest.

options.text: Guest workers move to postwar Western Europe
Early humans cross Beringia into the Americas
Enslaved Africans are forced across the Atlantic
Austronesian voyagers settle Pacific islands

explanation: Beringia came over 15,000 years ago, Austronesian voyages ~3000 BCE, the Atlantic trade in the 1500s, and guest workers after 1945.

trap_notes.default: Separate prehistoric peopling of continents from early modern forced migration and 20th-century labor migration.

prompt: Order John Borchert's four epochs of US urban growth from earliest to latest.

options.text: Auto-Air-Amenity era with highway suburbs
Sail-Wagon era along Atlantic ports
Steel-Rail era linking industrial cities
Iron Horse era of early steam railroads

explanation: Borchert traced US cities from Sail-Wagon (1790-1830) to Iron Horse (1830-1870), Steel-Rail (1870-1920), and Auto-Air-Amenity (1920+).

trap_notes.default: Follow the dominant transport technology: wooden ships and wagons, early iron rails, heavy steel rails, then cars and planes.

prompt: Order these supercontinent and mountain-building events from oldest to newest.

options.text: India collides with Asia to raise the Himalayas
Rodinia forms as an ancient supercontinent
Pangaea breaks into Laurasia and Gondwana
Pangaea assembles into one global landmass

explanation: Rodinia formed ~1B years ago, Pangaea assembled ~300M and split ~200M years ago, and the Himalayas rose ~50M years ago.

trap_notes.default: Rodinia predated Pangaea by hundreds of millions of years; the Himalayas rose after Pangaea split.

prompt: Order these navigation milestones from earliest to most recent.

options.text: Greenwich becomes the Prime Meridian
Harrison builds an accurate marine chronometer
Chinese sailors adopt the magnetic compass
LORAN radio beacons guide ocean ships

explanation: Chinese mariners used compasses by the 1000s, Harrison solved longitude in the 1760s, Greenwich was chosen in 1884, and LORAN began in WWII.

trap_notes.default: Place the magnetic compass in medieval China, the chronometer in the 1700s, Greenwich in 1884, and radio beacons in the 1940s.

prompt: Order the opening of these major shipping canals from earliest to latest.

options.text: Panama Canal links Atlantic and Pacific
Erie Canal connects Hudson River to Lake Erie
Suez Canal joins Mediterranean and Red Seas
Grand Canal links northern and southern China

explanation: China's Grand Canal was unified in 609 CE, the Erie Canal opened in 1825, the Suez Canal in 1869, and the Panama Canal in 1914.

trap_notes.default: Remember that Suez opened nearly 45 years before Panama, while the Erie Canal predated both.

prompt: Order these global agricultural milestones from earliest to most recent.

options.text: Green Revolution spreads high-yield wheat
Columbian Exchange swaps crops across oceans
Seed drills boost British crop rotation yields
Neolithic farmers domesticate wild grains

explanation: Farming began ~10,000 BCE, the Columbian Exchange after 1492, British farm advances in the 1700s, and the Green Revolution in the 1960s.

trap_notes.default: Place the Columbian Exchange before the 18th-century mechanical farming boom and the 1960s Green Revolution.

prompt: Order these US territorial acquisitions from earliest to most recent.

options.text: United States purchases Alaska from Russia
United States buys Louisiana Territory
Mexico cedes California and the Southwest
Republic of Texas joins the United States

explanation: The US bought Louisiana in 1803, annexed Texas in 1845, gained the Mexican Cession in 1848, and bought Alaska in 1867.

trap_notes.default: Texas annexation came three years before the Mexican Cession, and Alaska followed after the Civil War.

prompt: Order these river features from mountain headwaters to coastal mouth.

options.text: Sediment builds a fan-shaped coastal delta
Fast stream carves a steep V-shaped valley
Cut-off river bend forms an oxbow lake
Gentle slope creates broad river meanders

explanation: Rivers carve V-shaped valleys in steep uplands, meander across flat floodplains, pinch off oxbow lakes, and deposit deltas at the sea.

trap_notes.default: A river must first form wide meanders before a loop can pinch off into an oxbow lake.

prompt: Order the stages of primary ecological succession on bare volcanic rock.

options.text: Grasses and shrubs take root in thin soil
Lichens and mosses weather bare basalt
Mature shade-tolerant forest stabilizes
Cooled lava forms sterile rock surface

explanation: Primary succession starts on bare rock, then lichens form thin soil, grasses and shrubs root, and a mature forest stabilizes.

trap_notes.default: Pioneer species like lichens must create thin soil before rooted grasses and trees can survive.

prompt: Order these US environmental and conservation milestones from earliest to latest.

options.text: Congress passes the modern Clean Water Act
Yellowstone becomes the first national park
Dust Bowl prompts the Soil Conservation Service
US Forest Service forms under Gifford Pinchot

explanation: Yellowstone was established in 1872, the US Forest Service in 1905, the Soil Conservation Service in 1935, and the Clean Water Act in 1972.

trap_notes.default: Place Yellowstone in the 1870s, Progressive-Era forestry in 1905, Dust Bowl relief in the 1930s, and Clean Water Act in 1972.

prompt: Order the sequence of continental glacier advance and retreat.

options.text: Melting ice leaves behind moraines and kettle lakes
Heavy snow compacts into dense glacial ice
Advancing ice scours bedrock into U-shaped valleys
Warming climate causes the ice front to recede

explanation: Snow compacts into glacial ice, advancing glaciers carve valleys, warming triggers retreat, and meltwater leaves moraines and kettle lakes.

trap_notes.default: Glaciers must advance and scour rock before warming causes retreat and deposits moraines.

prompt: Order these global urbanization milestones from earliest to most recent.

options.text: Over half of the world lives in urban areas
First walled cities rise in Mesopotamia
New York and Tokyo pass ten million residents
Coal factories spark British industrial cities

explanation: Mesopotamian cities rose ~3500 BCE, British industrial cities in the 1800s, megacities in the 1950s, and a global urban majority in 2007.

trap_notes.default: The world's first megacities appeared in the mid-20th century, decades before the 2007 global urban majority.

prompt: Order these major phases of European overseas territorial control.

options.text: European powers partition Africa at Berlin
Asian and African colonies win independence
Spain conquers Aztec and Inca empires
Portugal sets up Atlantic island sugar posts

explanation: Portugal took Atlantic islands in the 1400s, Spain took the Americas in the 1500s, Africa was split in 1884, and colonies freed post-1945.

trap_notes.default: Separate 15th-16th century Atlantic empires from the late-19th century Scramble for Africa and post-1945 decolonization.

prompt: Order Darwin's stages of coral atoll formation from start to finish.

options.text: Sinking island leaves a wide lagoon barrier reef
Volcanic island rises above the tropical ocean
Ring-shaped coral atoll encircles open water
Fringing reef grows tight along the island shore

explanation: A volcanic island forms, a fringing reef hugs its shore, sinking widens a barrier lagoon, and only a coral atoll ring remains.

trap_notes.default: Remember the reef sequence: fringing reef (touching shore), barrier reef (lagoon gap), then atoll (island gone).

prompt: Order these global atmospheric and climate milestones from earliest to latest.

options.text: Paris Agreement sets global warming limits
Montreal Protocol phases out ozone-harming CFCs
Keeling begins Mauna Loa CO2 measurements
Kyoto Protocol sets binding emissions targets

explanation: Mauna Loa CO2 tracking began in 1958, the Montreal Protocol was signed in 1987, the Kyoto Protocol in 1997, and the Paris Agreement in 2015.

trap_notes.default: Ozone action (Montreal 1987) preceded the first global greenhouse treaty (Kyoto 1997) and Paris (2015).

prompt: Order these rock-cycle steps from molten magma to metamorphic rock.

options.text: Buried layers compact into sedimentary rock
Heat and pressure transform rock into gneiss
Molten magma cools into solid igneous rock
Weathering breaks rock into loose sand grains

explanation: Magma cools into igneous rock, weathering creates sediment, burial compacts sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure form gneiss.

trap_notes.default: Follow the mineral path: cooling magma -> loose sediment -> compacted rock -> heat-altered rock.

prompt: Order these major US internal migration waves from earliest to latest.

options.text: Retirees and workers surge into the Sun Belt
Pioneers travel Oregon Trail to the West
Black Southerners move to northern cities
Plains farm families flee Dust Bowl droughts

explanation: The Oregon Trail peaked in the 1840s, the Great Migration began around 1916, Dust Bowl moves in the 1930s, and Sun Belt growth after 1970.

trap_notes.default: Remember the Great Migration began during World War I, before the 1930s Dust Bowl and postwar Sun Belt boom.

prompt: Order the stages of rocky headland erosion by ocean waves.

options.text: Waves widen cliff cracks into a sea cave
Arch roof collapses leaving an isolated sea stack
Solid rocky headland juts into the sea
Cave breaks through headland to form a sea arch

explanation: Waves erode cracks in a rocky headland into a sea cave, cut through to create a sea arch, and collapse the arch into a sea stack.

trap_notes.default: Follow the erosion path: crack -> cave -> arch -> collapsed stack.

prompt: Order these dominant global energy sources from earliest to newest.

options.text: Petroleum fuels cars and highway freight
Wood and river waterwheels power early mills
Utility solar and wind farms expand rapidly
Coal drives steam engines and iron foundries

explanation: Wood and waterwheels came first, coal powered early factories, oil drove 20th-century transport, and renewables surged in the 2000s.

trap_notes.default: Coal preceded oil as the primary industrial fuel, while utility-scale wind and solar grew most recently.

prompt: Order these polar geography milestones from earliest to most recent.

options.text: Antarctic Treaty reserves continent for science
Roald Amundsen's team reaches the South Pole
Summer sea ice loss opens Northwest Passage
Fuchs completes first Antarctic land crossing

explanation: Amundsen reached the South Pole (1911), Fuchs crossed Antarctica (1958), the Antarctic Treaty signed (1959), and Arctic lanes opened (2007).

trap_notes.default: Early polar expeditions happened in the 1910s, scientific treaties in the late 1950s, and Arctic sea-ice opening in the 2000s.

prompt: Order the stages of soil horizon development from bare bedrock.

options.text: Decaying plants add dark humus to topsoil
Distinct O, A, B, and C horizons stabilize
Rain and frost crack solid bedrock
Deep mineral subsoil accumulates below surface

explanation: Weathering cracks bedrock, plants add humus to topsoil, leaching builds mineral subsoil, and mature soil horizons stabilize.

trap_notes.default: Bedrock must fracture first, then surface plants build humus before leaching differentiates deeper horizons.

prompt: Order these global trade network milestones from earliest to latest.

options.text: Standard shipping containers transform ports
Han Dynasty opens overland Silk Road routes
Portuguese ships sail around Cape of Good Hope
Arab dhows ride Indian Ocean monsoon winds

explanation: Han Silk Road opened ~130 BCE, monsoon dhow trade thrived in medieval times, da Gama rounded Africa in 1498, and containers began in 1956.

trap_notes.default: Overland Silk Road routes came first, followed by Indian Ocean dhow trade, European Cape routes, and modern container ships.

prompt: Order the lifecycle stages of a tropical hurricane.

options.text: Warm ocean water fuels rising moist air
Storm loses moisture and weakens over land
Rotating winds form a calm eye and eyewall
Tropical depression begins spinning slowly

explanation: Warm ocean heat feeds rising moist air, creating a spinning depression that grows into an eyewall hurricane before weakening overland.

trap_notes.default: Hurricanes need warm ocean fuel to organize into a depression and eyewall before losing power at landfall.

prompt: Order these spatial analysis and GIS milestones from earliest to latest.

options.text: Landsat 1 captures digital Earth imagery
Crowdsourced web maps update in real time
John Snow maps London cholera water pumps
Desktop GIS software layers census data

explanation: John Snow mapped cholera in 1854, Landsat 1 launched in 1972, desktop GIS spread in the 1990s, and live web maps arrived in the 2000s.

trap_notes.default: John Snow's paper map came in 1854; satellite imagery began in 1972 before personal desktop GIS and web maps.

prompt: Order the steps that create karst caves and sinkholes.

options.text: Weakly acidic groundwater dissolves limestone
Weakened cave roof collapses into a sinkhole
Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from soil
Underground rock gaps widen into caverns

explanation: Rainwater picks up carbon dioxide to become acidic, dissolves buried limestone, carves caverns, and eventually collapses into a sinkhole.

trap_notes.default: Water must become acidic and dissolve limestone into caverns before the ground above can collapse.

prompt: Order these world population milestones from earliest to most recent.

options.text: Global population reaches 5 billion people
Global population reaches 1 billion people
Global population reaches 8 billion people
Global population reaches 2 billion people

explanation: World population reached 1 billion around 1804, 2 billion in 1927, 5 billion in 1987, and 8 billion in 2022.

trap_notes.default: Human population grew sequentially from 1 to 2 to 5 to 8 billion between 1804 and 2022.

prompt: Order the stages as a glacial lake gradually turns into a meadow.

options.text: Reeds and cattails fill shallow water edges
Deep cold basin holds clear glacial water
Dry organic soil supports meadow grasses
Runoff silt and algae build up on lakebed

explanation: A deep glacial lake traps runoff silt and organic matter, becomes shallow enough for reeds, and eventually fills in as a dry meadow.

trap_notes.default: Sediment must shallow the basin before marsh plants can root across it and turn it into dry meadow.

prompt: Order these US federal land and water milestones from earliest to latest.

options.text: Hoover Dam creates Lake Mead reservoir
Homestead Act grants western farm plots
Wild and Scenic Rivers Act protects streams
Reclamation Act funds western irrigation

explanation: The Homestead Act passed in 1862, Reclamation Act in 1902, Hoover Dam finished in 1936, and the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act in 1968.

trap_notes.default: Homesteading came in the 1860s, federal irrigation policy in 1902, Hoover Dam in the 1930s, and river protection in 1968.

prompt: Order the typical stages of urban neighborhood gentrification.

options.text: Rising rents displace longtime working families
Factory closures leave cheap, aging housing
Developers renovate homes and upscale shops
Artists and students move in for low rents

explanation: Factory closures lower rents, attracting artists; developers then renovate homes, raising rents and displacing longtime residents.

trap_notes.default: Low rents attract early newcomers before large-scale renovation and rent-driven displacement occur.

prompt: Order these milestones in global time-zone standardization.

options.text: International conference sets 24 global zones
Each town sets clocks by its own solar noon
Atomic clocks anchor Coordinated Universal Time
US railroads adopt four standard time zones

explanation: Towns used local solar time until US railroads adopted standard zones in 1883, the world conference met in 1884, and UTC began in the 1960s.

trap_notes.default: Railroads standardized US time in 1883 right before the 1884 global conference, while atomic UTC came in the 1960s.

prompt: Order the stages of desertification in a semiarid grassland.

options.text: Exposed topsoil dries and blows away in wind
Barren sand and hardpan replace farmland
Overgrazing and woodcutting strip grass cover
Gullies form as rare rains wash bare ground

explanation: Clearing grass cover exposes soil to wind erosion, rare storms carve gullies, and the degraded land turns barren.

trap_notes.default: Vegetation loss comes first, exposing soil to wind and water erosion until barren desert remains.

prompt: Order these turning points in European political geography.

options.text: Iron Curtain divides Western and Eastern blocs
Treaty of Westphalia defines sovereign states
Maastricht Treaty creates the European Union
Congress of Vienna redraws post-Napoleon map

explanation: Westphalia (1648) defined states, Vienna (1815) redrew Europe, the Iron Curtain divided it after 1945, and the EU formed in 1993.

trap_notes.default: Anchor Westphalia in 1648, Vienna in 1815, the Cold War after 1945, and the Maastricht EU in 1993.

prompt: Order the steps that build an alluvial fan at a mountain base.

options.text: Stream exits narrow canyon onto flat valley
Fast mountain stream carries gravel downstream
Fan-shaped wedge of sediment spreads outward
Slowing water drops heavy boulders and sand

explanation: A steep stream carries gravel, exits the canyon onto a flat valley, slows down to drop sediment, and builds a fan-shaped deposit.

trap_notes.default: Sediment is carried in the steep canyon, dropped when the stream hits the flat floor, and shaped into a fan.

prompt: Order these stages of Pacific Island settlement from earliest to latest.

options.text: Maori voyagers settle Aotearoa New Zealand
Lapita seafarers reach Fiji and western islands
Polynesians reach Hawaii and Easter Island
Distinct Polynesian culture forms in Samoa

explanation: Lapita settlers reached Fiji ~1000 BCE, Samoa/Tonga came next, voyagers reached Hawaii by ~1000 CE, and Maori settled New Zealand ~1250 CE.

trap_notes.default: Polynesian settlement moved eastward from Fiji and Samoa to Hawaii, with New Zealand settled last around 1250 CE.

prompt: Order these phases of North American suburban growth from earliest to latest.

options.text: Edge cities cluster offices at beltway exits
Streetcar lines create narrow commuter suburbs
Postwar tract homes spread along new highways
Regional shopping malls anchor suburban towns

explanation: Streetcar suburbs grew around 1900, postwar tracts in the 1950s, regional malls in the 1960s-70s, and edge cities in the 1980s-90s.

trap_notes.default: Streetcars preceded postwar car suburbs, which later gained regional malls and finally independent edge cities.

prompt: Order these global wildlife and habitat milestones from earliest to latest.

options.text: CITES restricts cross-border wildlife trade
IUCN launches global Red List of species
Nations adopt 30x30 biodiversity protection goal
Ramsar Convention protects global wetlands

explanation: The IUCN Red List began in 1964, Ramsar wetlands treaty in 1971, CITES wildlife trade treaty in 1975, and the 30x30 goal in 2022.

trap_notes.default: The Red List (1964) came first, followed by Ramsar (1971), CITES (1975), and the 2022 30x30 framework.

prompt: Order the path of air crossing a coastal mountain range.

options.text: Dry air descends the leeward slope and warms
Cooling vapor condenses into windward rain
Moist ocean air is forced up mountain slopes
Warm dry air creates a rain-shadow desert

explanation: Moist ocean air rises up the windward slope, cools to drop rain, descends the leeward side dry, and forms a rain shadow.

trap_notes.default: Air must rise and drop its moisture on the windward side before descending dry on the leeward side.

prompt: Order these landmark geographic projects in China from earliest to latest.

options.text: Three Gorges Dam spans the Yangtze River
Grand Canal links Yangtze and Yellow rivers
High-speed rail network links major cities
Qin Dynasty connects northern frontier walls

explanation: Qin walls were linked ~214 BCE, the Grand Canal in 609 CE, Three Gorges Dam finished in 2006, and high-speed rail boomed after 2008.

trap_notes.default: Great Wall unification came in BCE, the Grand Canal in the Sui Dynasty, Three Gorges in 2006, and high-speed rail after 2008.

prompt: Order how a sandy barrier island migrates landward as sea level rises.

options.text: Dune grasses anchor fresh sand on backshore
Storm waves wash ocean sand over the island
Entire sandbar shifts closer to the mainland
New marshland builds along the lagoon edge

explanation: Storm overwash pushes sand across the island, building new lagoon marshland and vegetated dunes as the whole island rolls landward.

trap_notes.default: Storm overwash moves sand onto the back side first, allowing marshes and dunes to rebuild inland.

prompt: Order these ocean exploration and seafloor mapping milestones.

options.text: Argo robotic floats track ocean heat worldwide
HMS Challenger measures deep-ocean trenches
Alvin submersible discovers deep-sea vents
Sonar charts the Mid-Atlantic Ridge rift

explanation: HMS Challenger sailed in 1872, sonar mapped ridges in the 1950s, Alvin found vents in 1977, and Argo floats deployed in 2000.

trap_notes.default: Challenger used weighted lines in the 1870s, sonar came in the 1950s, Alvin in 1977, and robotic Argo floats in 2000.

prompt: Order four stages of Rostow's Modernization Model of economic growth.

options.text: Rapid factory growth drives industrial takeoff
Subsistence farming dominates traditional society
High mass consumption of consumer goods
New roads and schools set stage for takeoff

explanation: Rostow's model moves from traditional society to preconditions for takeoff, industrial takeoff, and finally high mass consumption.

trap_notes.default: Infrastructure preconditions precede industrial takeoff, which precedes a mass-consumption service economy.

prompt: Order the historical stages of the Aral Sea environmental crisis.

options.text: Salt flats and toxic dust replace dry seabed
Kokaral Dam partially restores the North Aral
Soviet canals divert rivers to cotton fields
Shrinking water splits the sea into two basins

explanation: Soviet canals diverted rivers in the 1960s, splitting the sea by 1987, leaving salt flats, until the 2005 Kokaral Dam aided the north.

trap_notes.default: River diversion caused the sea to split and dry into salt flats before the 2005 dam restored the northern basin.

prompt: Order the sequence of a desert arroyo flash flood.

options.text: Wall of muddy water surges down narrow canyon
Cloudburst drops heavy rain on baked soil
Floodwater sinks into dry downstream sand
Unabsorbed runoff funnels into a dry wash

explanation: Heavy rain hits baked soil, funnels into a dry wash, surges downstream as a flash flood, and eventually sinks into sandy flats.

trap_notes.default: Runoff must funnel into the canyon before a flood wall surges downstream and later soaks into flat sand.

prompt: Sort each coordinate-grid trait into Latitude or Longitude.
explanation: Latitude lines (parallels) measure north-south from the Equator, while longitude lines (meridians) converge at the poles.

trap_notes.default: Latitude lines run east-west to measure north-south; longitude lines run pole-to-pole to measure east-west.

items.text: Layers roads, soil, and census data

prompt: Classify each geospatial function under GIS or GPS.
explanation: GPS uses satellites to determine exact location, while GIS is software that layers and analyzes spatial data.

trap_notes.default: GPS finds where you are; GIS layers and analyzes multiple map datasets.

items.text: Mild winters moderated by ocean air
Cool summers with frequent sea fog

prompt: Sort each climate trait into Maritime Climate or Continental Climate.
explanation: Oceans heat and cool slowly, giving maritime coasts mild seasons, whereas inland continental areas face extreme temperature swings.

trap_notes.default: Water buffers coastal temperatures; interior landmasses heat up and cool down rapidly.

items.text: Often preserves plant or shell fossils
Built from compacted sand or mud

prompt: Classify each rock trait under Igneous Rock or Sedimentary Rock.
explanation: Igneous rocks crystallize from cooled magma or lava, whereas sedimentary rocks form from compacted layers that can hold fossils.

trap_notes.default: Heat melts away fossils in igneous rocks; gentle layered burial preserves fossils in sedimentary rocks.

items.text: Encloses another nation on all sides
Lacks direct access to any ocean
Relies on neighbors for sea ports

prompt: Match each territorial trait to Perforated State or Landlocked State.
explanation: A perforated state completely surrounds another country, while a landlocked state has no ocean coastline.

trap_notes.default: South Africa is perforated by Lesotho; Lesotho (or Bolivia) is landlocked without a sea coast.

items.text: Suits large, diverse nations like US
Local units carry out national laws

prompt: Sort each governance trait into Unitary State or Federal State.
explanation: Unitary states concentrate authority in a central government, whereas federal states share constitutional power with regional units.

trap_notes.default: Unitary means one central authority; federal means power is constitutionally shared with provinces or states.

items.text: High labor input on small plots
Low input spread over huge ranches

prompt: Classify each farming practice as Intensive or Extensive Agriculture.
explanation: Intensive farming uses heavy labor or capital per acre on small plots, while extensive farming uses vast land with lower inputs per acre.

trap_notes.default: Compare effort per acre: dense rice terraces are intensive; sprawling cattle ranches are extensive.

items.text: Brings new outside money into city

prompt: Sort each urban business trait into Basic Industry or Nonbasic Industry.
explanation: Basic industries sell outside the city to bring in new income, while nonbasic businesses circulate money locally.

trap_notes.default: Ask where the customers live: outside buyers mean basic; local neighbors mean nonbasic.

items.text: One city dwarfs all others in nation
Second city has half the top size
Bangkok or Paris leading its country

prompt: Match each urban-system trait to Primate City or Rank-Size Rule.
explanation: A primate city is more than twice as large as the next city, whereas the rank-size rule predicts proportional city sizes (1/2, 1/3, 1/4).

trap_notes.default: Primate city systems are top-heavy; rank-size systems step down smoothly by fractions.

items.text: Rings expand around one city core
Airports and campuses form separate nodes

prompt: Classify each urban layout under Concentric Zone or Multiple Nuclei Model.
explanation: Burgess's Concentric Zone Model radiates in rings from one CBD, while Harris and Ullman's Multiple Nuclei Model centers on several hubs.

trap_notes.default: Concentric means bullseye rings around one center; multiple nuclei means several distinct activity centers.

items.text: Can safely return to home country

prompt: Sort each migration description into Refugee or Economic Migrant.
explanation: Refugees flee danger or persecution and receive international protection, while economic migrants move voluntarily for work.

trap_notes.default: Distinguish forced flight from danger (refugee) from voluntary relocation for jobs (economic migrant).

items.text: Includes men and children in denominator

prompt: Match each demographic metric to Crude Birth Rate or Total Fertility Rate.
explanation: Crude Birth Rate counts yearly births per 1,000 total residents, while Total Fertility Rate estimates lifetime births per woman.

trap_notes.default: Crude Birth Rate uses the whole population as its base; Total Fertility Rate focuses on women's lifetime births.

items.text: Dense spruce and pine boreal forest
Largest land biome across Canada, Russia
Covered by mosses, lichens, and sedges

prompt: Sort each cold-climate trait into Tundra Biome or Taiga Biome.
explanation: Tundra is treeless and underlain by permafrost, whereas taiga (boreal forest) supports vast evergreen conifer trees.

trap_notes.default: Tundra means treeless polar plains; taiga means the northern evergreen conifer forest.

items.text: Multiple threads split around gravel bars
Flows slowly across flat muddy plains

prompt: Classify each river pattern as Meandering River or Braided River.
explanation: Meandering rivers wind as one channel across flat floodplains, while braided rivers split into many channels around excess gravel.

trap_notes.default: Meandering is one looping channel; braided is many interwoven streams choked with gravel.

items.text: Relies on high-yield hybrid grain seeds
Builds soil with compost and cover crops

prompt: Sort each agricultural practice into Green Revolution or Organic Farming.
explanation: The Green Revolution boosted yields using hybrid seeds and synthetic inputs, whereas organic farming relies on natural soil builders.

trap_notes.default: Despite its name, the Green Revolution used synthetic fertilizers and bred hybrids; organic farming avoids synthetic chemicals.
